newsitem.title: USA: Unabomber suspect trial set for year from now.
newsitem.headline: Unabomber suspect trial set for year from now.

text.p: The trial of Unabomber suspect Theodore Kaczynski on charges of carrying out four bombings, two of them deadly, will not begin until almost a year from now, a federal judge ruled on Friday.

U.S. District Judge Garland Burrell said Kaczynski's trial will start on November 12, 1997, more than 18 months after he was arrested, with matted hair and torn jeans, at his rustic one-room cabin in Montana.

Kaczynski, jailed in Sacramento, was accused of being the shadowy Unabomber, who killed three people and injured 23 during an anti-technology bombing campaign between 1978 and 1995. The Unabomber targeted scientists and business executives by planting or mailing lovingly hand-crafted bombs.

Kaczynski, 54, appeared in court for the first time on Friday since he was arraigned in Sacramento in June. His image was transformed from the bedraggled hermit who was arrested in Montana last April.

Wearing a brown tweed jacket and with hair and beard well-groomed, he looked like the mathematics professor he once was. He seemed relaxed as he sat between his attorneys, chatting with them and smiling from time to time.
Prosecutors, eager to get on with the case, had suggested a May 1997 trial date in court papers but, after the defence sought more time, suggested a September 1997 start.

Kaczynski's attorneys argued for a November 1997 date if the judge insisted on setting a date, but said they would prefer that he wait until next June to set a trial date when they would have a clearer idea of the time needed to prepare.
"It's just a huge case. It's a monster case, like a huge anti-trust case in terms of documents, information and investigative leads," defence attorney Quin Denvir said.

Defence attorneys have to sift through a vast amount of evidence turned over by prosecutors, including thousands of pages of documents and photographs gathered during the FBI's painstaking 17-year investigation.

Kaczynski pleaded not guilty to Sacramento charges accusing him of four bomb attacks between 1985 and 1995 that killed timber industry lobbyist Gilbert Murray and computer store owner Hugh Scrutton and injured two prominent scientists. Prosecutors said they expect the trial to last three to four months and have not said if they will seek the death penalty.

Asked how Kaczynski was feeling, Denvir told reporters outside court: "He's doing well enough given the fact that he's in a big-city jail. He's getting along." He said Kaczynski was helping his attorneys.
Kaczynski has been indicted separately in New Jersey on charges that he mailed a bomb that killed advertising executive Thomas Mosser in December 1994.
